title: Brutalism
objective: After this level you can explain raw concrete buildings and why people argue about them.
summary: Brutalism comes from béton brut, raw concrete, not from brutal. Banham praised buildings made of what they appear to be made of; fans see post-war ambition, critics a dystopia.

cards.headline: One building: 'elephant droppings' to a prince, Stonehenge to a writer.
cards.body: Portsmouth's Tricorn Centre opened in 1966, and the critic Ian Nairn cheered: "At last there is something to shout about in Portsmouth." Prince Charles later called it "a mildewed lump of elephant droppings"; the writer Jonathan Meades compared it to Stonehenge. It was demolished in 2004. Welcome to Brutalism.

cards.headline: Not brutal: raw
cards.body: The name doesn't come from brutal. It probably comes from béton brut, French for raw concrete, Le Corbusier's phrase while building his Unité d'Habitation in 1952. Yes, Level 73's machine-for-living man. From the 1950s he left his materials unfinished, including concrete still printed with the marks of the formwork it was cast in. You can read how a wall was made just by looking at it.

cards.headline: Made of what it appears to be made of
cards.body: In a 1955 essay, the critic Reyner Banham named a trend in British architecture "The New Brutalism". His model was a school at Hunstanton by Alison and Peter Smithson: a building "made of what it appears to be made of". No decoration, nothing hidden. And it wasn't only concrete. The Smithsons wanted every material, brick, timber or glass, honestly expressed.

mascot.line: Brutalism's test is simple: if it looks like concrete, it had better be concrete.

cards.headline: Loved and loathed
cards.body: Historic England calls Brutalism loved and loathed, one of the most controversial styles of the 20th century. To its fans, it shows the post-war drive to rebuild towns so they served people better. To its critics, it was a dystopian landscape-destroyer. The Tricorn's fans and foes were looking at the same raw concrete and seeing opposite things.

cards.headline: Brutalism: unfinished, on purpose
learned: The Tricorn Centre: praised, reviled, demolished
Béton brut: French for raw concrete
Banham (1955): made of what it appears to be made of
Loved and loathed: post-war ambition or dystopia

questions.prompt: Where does the name Brutalism most probably come from?

options.label: The word brutal, for its harsh looks
An architect named Brut
options.rationale: It comes from a French phrase.

options.label: Béton brut, French for raw concrete

questions.explanation: The name probably comes from béton brut, French for raw concrete, Le Corbusier's phrase.

questions.prompt: Why did Reyner Banham single out the Smithsons' school at Hunstanton?

options.label: It was the tallest concrete building in Britain
options.rationale: Banham praised its honesty, not its height.

options.label: It was made of what it appears to be made of
It was covered in rich decoration
It hid its structure behind smooth panels
options.rationale: Its structure and materials were on show.

questions.explanation: Banham praised Hunstanton as a building 'made of what it appears to be made of', with materials honestly shown.

questions.prompt: Level 1's Vitruvius said good building needs delight. Why is Brutalism such a hard case for that test?

options.label: Brutalist buildings have no uses
options.rationale: They served many uses; the argument is about beauty.

options.label: Fans find it beautiful; critics find it monstrous

questions.explanation: Delight means beauty, and Brutalism is loved and loathed: fans see ambition, critics a dystopian landscape-destroyer.
